## 9. Recommendation (D1-D3)

**NO-GO on building any token-reduction feature. No tickets filed.**

The category splits cleanly once you sort by mechanism, and archy's position in
each half is already settled:

- **Prefix bloat** (tool definitions). The one real, independently measured
  problem. **archy already solved its share** (#227, #265) and now measures
  **3,918 model-visible tokens, 1.96% of a 200k window, ~356 tokens per tool**.
  The platform has also moved underneath it: Claude Code defers MCP tools by
  default. Nothing to build.
- **Comprehension context** (briefs, maps, retrieval). Unmeasured by its own
  vendors, and the one rigorous compression study reports **42% fewer tokens
  for −12pp resolution rate**. archy tested its version twice and got null.
  Nothing to build that we have reason to believe would work.

### D1. The gates, applied to every candidate

| candidate | anti-theater | discriminant | usage signal | beats the null? | verdict |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `archy brief` / repo map (redo) | Fails. Measured null already; the strongest precedent (aider) publishes no token evidence | No | None | **No.** Nothing addresses the measured zero headroom | **Wontfix** |
| Compress archy's tool descriptions further | Passes (deterministic, in-repo measurable) | Marginal | None | n/a | **Not worth it.** 1.96% is already lean; effort better spent elsewhere |
| Trim `outputSchema` | **Fails on premise.** It is client-side payload, not model context (§7) | No | None | n/a | **Wontfix** |
| Token-savings marketing claim | Fails hard. We have two nulls of our own | No | None | No | **Forbidden.** See §14c.7 |
| Structural-Q&A footprint bench | Passes (falsifiable, real headroom per §8) | Yes | **None** | **Yes**, different task class | **Recorded as reopen path, not scheduled** |

### D2. The call, and why

**Do not build.** Three independent reasons, any one sufficient:

1. **The available surface is spent.** Of ten categories, only three are a
   static analyzer's to build (§5). Two are shipped. The third is measured
   null, twice.
2. **The headline numbers do not survive their baselines.** 99.9% is against a
   1.17M-token configuration nobody ships; 98.7% is arithmetic on one
   constructed example; 95% is against reading an entire repo. And caching
   already took most of the cost win those numbers describe, overstating real
   savings by up to 10x for cached prefixes (§4).
3. **Zero usage signal.** `ADOPTERS.md` is empty, every issue is
   maintainer-authored, and nobody has asked archy to reduce their token bill.
   This is hype-motivated, which is precisely the case gate 3 exists to catch.

**What archy should say instead.** The honest positioning, consistent with
§14c.7: archy is a deterministic structural checker. It catches cycles, layer
violations, and score regressions an agent would otherwise introduce. It does
not claim to make agent runs cheaper, because we tested that and could not show
it.

### D3. Tickets

**None filed.** Nothing cleared all four gates.

### The reopen path, recorded so this is not re-proposed from scratch

§8 supplies, for the first time, a real answer to gate 4 ("why would it beat
the null?"): **task class**. Every archy footprint study to date used an
**editing** task, where the graph is a hint and the measured headroom was zero.
codegraph's benchmark shows a large effect on **structural question answering**,
where the graph *is* the answer, and archy already ships the tools that would
serve it (`archy_impact`, `archy_graph(focus=)`, `archy_cycles`).

If this is ever revisited, the design is:

> **Arm D, structural Q&A.** Fix a set of structural questions with verifiable
> answers ("what breaks if I change X?", "what are the cycles through Y?",
> "what is the blast radius of Z?"). Compare an agent answering them with the
> archy MCP server available vs with only grep/read. Measure tool calls, file
> reads, and tokens to a *correct* answer, scoring correctness explicitly so a
> fast wrong answer cannot win. Use a large, tangled repo, since §8 reports the

## 9. Recommendation (D1-D3)

**NO-GO on building any token-reduction feature. No tickets filed.**

The category splits cleanly once you sort by mechanism, and archy's position in
each half is already settled:

- **Prefix bloat** (tool definitions). The one real, independently measured
  problem. **archy already solved its share** (#227, #265) and now measures
  **3,918 model-visible tokens, 1.96% of a 200k window, ~356 tokens per tool**.
  The platform has also moved underneath it: Claude Code defers MCP tools by
  default. Nothing to build.
- **Comprehension context** (briefs, maps, retrieval). Unmeasured by its own
  vendors, and the one rigorous compression study reports **42% fewer tokens
  for −12pp resolution rate**. archy tested its version twice and got null.
  Nothing to build that we have reason to believe would work.

### D1. The gates, applied to every candidate

| Trim `outputSchema` | **Fails on premise.** It is client-side payload, not model context (§7) | No | None | n/a | **Wontfix** |
| Token-savings marketing claim | Fails hard. We have two nulls of our own | No | None | No | **Forbidden.** See §14c.7 |
| Structural-Q&A footprint bench | Passes (falsifiable, real headroom per §8) | Yes | **None** | **Yes**, different task class | **Recorded as reopen path, not scheduled** |

**Do not build.** Three independent reasons, any one sufficient:

1. **The available surface is spent.** Of ten categories, only three are a
   static analyzer's to build (§5). Two are shipped. The third is measured
   null, twice.
2. **The headline numbers do not survive their baselines.** 99.9% is against a
   1.17M-token configuration nobody ships; 98.7% is arithmetic on one
   constructed example; 95% is against reading an entire repo. And caching
   already took most of the cost win those numbers describe, overstating real
   savings by up to 10x for cached prefixes (§4).

   maintainer-authored, and nobody has asked archy to reduce their token bill.
   This is hype-motivated, which is precisely the case gate 3 exists to catch.

## Sources

Tiered by what kind of evidence they are. This tiering is the point of the
whole file: most of the category's famous numbers sit in the bottom tier.

### Independent / peer-reviewable measurement

- Hrubec & Cito, *Reducing Token Usage of State-in-Context Agents using
  Minification*, arXiv [2606.01326](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01326) (May
  2026). Independent replication, SWE-bench Verified, GPT-5-mini. **42% fewer
  input tokens, −12pp resolution rate.** The single most important source here.
- Fan et al., *SWE-Effi: Re-Evaluating Software AI Agent System Effectiveness
  Under Resource Constraints*, arXiv
  [2509.09853](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.09853). Establishes agent cost as an
  evaluation axis.
- Chroma, [*Context Rot*](https://research.trychroma.com/context-rot). 18 LLMs;
  non-uniform degradation with input length; a single distractor measurably
  hurts. Replication code published.
- Community measurement on
  [claude-code issue #11364](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/11364):
  seven MCP servers, **67,300 tokens of tool definitions, 33.7% of a 200k
  window**. The one non-strawman baseline in the prefix-bloat half.

### Vendor benchmarks (methodology published, vendor-run)

- [codegraph](https://github.com/colbymchenry/codegraph). 7 repos, 7 languages,
  Claude Code headless, median of 4 runs per arm. 89% fewer tool calls, 69%
  fewer tokens. **Scope: answering one architecture question**, not editing.
  Publishes its own weak spots and measured per-language coverage.
- Anthropic, [Tool Search Tool](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/advanced-tool-use)
  (Nov 2025). "85% reduction in token usage."

### Vendor claims (illustrative arithmetic or unquantified)

- Anthropic, [code execution with MCP](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/code-execution-with-mcp).
  "150,000 tokens to 2,000 tokens, a saving of 98.7%", from **one constructed
  example**.
- Cloudflare, [Code Mode](https://blog.cloudflare.com/code-mode/) and the Feb
  2026 follow-up. "99.9%", against 2,500+ endpoints at an estimated 1.17M
  tokens, a configuration that cannot be run.
- [CodeScene CodeHealth MCP](https://codescene.com/product/code-health-mcp).
  "Up to 45% fewer tokens burned." Evidence rendered as images.
- [jCodeMunch `TOKEN_SAVINGS.md`](https://github.com/jgravelle/jcodemunch-mcp/blob/main/TOKEN_SAVINGS.md).
  "~95%+", baseline = reading the whole repository.
- [serena](https://github.com/oraios/serena). Efficiency asserted in prose, no
  numbers.
- [aider repo map](https://aider.chat/docs/repomap.html) and the
  [tree-sitter writeup](https://aider.chat/2023/10/22/repomap.html). Mechanism
  documented, **no token measurement published**; the
  [benchmark](https://aider.chat/docs/benchmarks.html) is 133 single-file
  Exercism exercises scored on pass rate.
- [repomix](https://repomix.com/guide/). Counts tokens, does not reduce them.

### Platform mechanics (primary documentation)

- Anthropic, [prompt caching](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-caching).
  Cache write 1.25x (5m) / 2x (1h); **cache hit 0.1x**.
- Anthropic, [Agent Skills](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/overview).
  Progressive disclosure; unused bundled files "cost zero tokens".
- Anthropic, [effective context engineering](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents).
  Compaction, note-taking, sub-agents; sub-agent distillate "often 1,000-2,000
  tokens".
- [Claude Code MCP docs](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/claude-code/mcp).
  Tool search on by default, MCP tools deferred; `auto` mode uses a 10%
  context-window threshold.
- [MCP specification, Tools](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/server/tools).
  `outputSchema` semantics.
- Anthropic [tool use overview](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/agents-and-tools/tool-use/overview).
  Tool definitions carry `name`, `description`, `input_schema`; **no
  output-schema field**, which is what makes §7's correction necessary.

### archy's own evidence

- [`RESEARCH_METRICS.md`](RESEARCH_METRICS.md) §14c.6, §14c.7.
- [`PREWALK_READ_REDUCTION_SYNTHESIS.md`](PREWALK_READ_REDUCTION_SYNTHESIS.md).
- [`../../bench/agent_footprint_results.md`](../../bench/agent_footprint_results.md)
  (#282 N=10, #289 N=22, both null).
- Direct measurement of archy's own MCP surface, this file §7, reproducible via
  `create_server().list_tools()` plus `tiktoken`.

7	measured, and archy already solved its share) and comprehension context

9	null). No tickets filed.

11	## The question
12	
13	Tools, harnesses, and skills increasingly claim to reduce the token usage of
14	coding agents. What mechanisms are those claims actually based on? Which are
15	measured and which are marketing? And does it make sense for archy to ship
16	anything in this category?

18	archy has a strong and uncomfortable prior here, recorded in

20	token-reduction propositions at its own layer and both returned null.**

23	  measured agent footprint. `footprint_tokens` median **+4,213 in the

26	  median **−2.0** (14/8, **p=0.286**), after an N=10 hint at p=0.109 that did

30	failed twice, is there a mechanism in this space that we have not tested and
31	that would survive our own gates?** A no-go is the expected outcome and a fine
32	one.

35

37	   or is it advice dressed as a feature? (Templates: §14c.6, and the #288 /
38	   #298 non-results.)
39	2. **OECD / discriminant validity**: does it measure something archy does not
40	   already measure, and is it actionable?
41	3. **Usage signal**: is anyone asking, or is this paper/hype-motivated?
42	   (Baseline: `ADOPTERS.md` is empty; every issue is maintainer-authored.)
43	4. **Beat the null**: any proposed mechanism must explain why it would succeed
44	   where #282 and #289 failed.

50	      context compaction / summarization, retrieval over code (RAG, embeddings),
51	      sub-agent context isolation, tool-surface reduction, progressive disclosure
52	      (skills / lazy-loaded instructions), repo packing (repomix-style), code
53	      maps / skeletons / outlines (tree-sitter, ctags), LSP-backed navigation,
54	      diff-scoped context, output-format compression, prompt caching.
55	- [x] A2. For each category, name 2-4 concrete tools/products and what exactly
56	      they claim, quoted, with the source.
57	- [x] A3. For each, state the **mechanism**: what physically removes tokens?
58	      (fewer files read, shorter representation of the same files, cache hits,
59	      fewer turns, smaller tool schemas, deferred loading.)
60

63	      N, baseline, model, task set. Which are bare assertions?
64	- [x] B2. Any independent replication or third-party benchmark? (Look for
65	      adversarial or negative results specifically, not just vendor blogs.)
66	- [x] B3. What do the negative / null results in the literature say? (e.g.
67	      context-rot and "more context hurts" findings, the bitter-lesson claims
68	      already cited in §14c.6.)

70	      same prefix is cheap. Does "input token reduction" still mean what these
71	      tools imply? What is the right cost metric (cache-read vs cache-write vs
72	      output)? Note archy's own finding that `pre_edit_input_tokens` was
73	      near-useless under caching.
74	
75	### Part C: does any mechanism apply to archy
76	- [x] C1. Which mechanisms are even available to a *static dependency-graph*
77	      tool, as opposed to a harness or an editor?
78	- [x] C2. For each available mechanism, why would it beat #282 / #289? Be
79	      specific about what was wrong with those designs (easy/grep-able task,
80	      brief precision 0.33, no headroom because the agent found the 3-file
81	      spine unaided) and whether the mechanism addresses it.
82	- [x] C3. What does archy already ship that is in this category but not
83	      marketed as such? (MCP surface consolidation #227/#265 shrank
84	      always-in-context tool schemas; `response_format="summary"` defaults;
85	      DSM summary ~89% smaller.) Is the honest position "we already did the
86	      only version that works"?
87	- [x] C4. Competitive check: do comparable static-analysis / graph tools ship
88	      token-reduction features, and is there evidence they work?
89	
90	### Part D: the call
91	- [x] D1. Apply the four gates to every surviving candidate.
92	- [x] D2. Write the go / no-go in §9 with reasons, and if no-go, record the
93	      reopen path so this does not get re-proposed.
94	- [x] D3. File follow-up tickets only if a candidate clears all four gates.
95	
96	## 1. Landscape (A1-A3)
97	
98	Ten categories. The column that matters is **mechanism**: what physically
99	removes tokens. Sorting by mechanism rather than by product collapses most of
100	the marketing into four real levers (substitute a smaller representation, defer
101	loading, isolate context, shrink the always-resident prefix) plus one category
102	that reduces nothing and one that changes cost without changing tokens.
103	
104	| # | category | examples | mechanism: what actually removes tokens |
105	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
106	| 1 | **Repo packing** | repomix, gitingest, code2prompt | **None.** Serializes a repo into one blob. 108	| 3 | **Symbol-level retrieval (LSP)** | serena, JetBrains/LSP MCP servers | Read a symbol and its references instead of whole files. |
109	| 4 | **Progressive disclosure** | Anthropic Agent Skills | Only `name` + `description` sit in the system prompt; SKILL.md loads on trigger; bundled files "stay on the filesystem and cost zero tokens" until read. |
110	| 5 | **Compaction / summarization** | Claude Code `/compact`, memory tool | Replace a long history with a summary and reinitialize. Costs a summarization call to save future turns. |

113	| 8 | **Output-format efficiency** | token-efficient tool use, concise response formats | Same information, fewer tokens on the wire. archy ships `response_format="summary"` defaults; DSM summary is ~89% smaller. |
114	| 9 | **Code retrieval / embeddings** | Cursor-style codebase indexing | Fetch ranked chunks instead of whole files. |
115	| 10 | **Prompt caching** | Anthropic prompt caching | **Reduces cost, not tokens.** The prefix is still sent and still occupies context; it is billed differently. See §4. |
116

# Research

Curated, published research behind archy's design decisions: the literature survey and the empirical studies that gate which metrics ship, get deferred, or get rejected. These are the version-controlled, citable counterparts to raw working notes; they are referenced from the [README](../../README.md), [`ROADMAP.md`](../ROADMAP.md), and [`FUTURE.md`](../FUTURE.md).

| Doc | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| [`RESEARCH_METRICS.md`](RESEARCH_METRICS.md) | The literature survey: ~15 architecture-quality metrics evaluated for Python-specific applicability, plus the AI-agent-feedback section (§14) tying archy to the 2025-2026 coding-agent research (Navigation Paradox, LocAgent, Constraint Decay). The catalogue that informs the roadmap. |
| [`AXIS_REVIEW.md`](AXIS_REVIEW.md) | The OECD composite-indicator framework applied to every score-axis-promotion decision (why 5 axes, why `calls_per_edge` is not a 6th). |
| [`CALL_WEIGHTED_Q_EMPIRICS.md`](CALL_WEIGHTED_Q_EMPIRICS.md) | Empirical study behind v0.21's call-weighted Newman Q diagnostic (why it ships as a parallel diagnostic, not an axis replacement). |
| [`DSM_EMPIRICS.md`](DSM_EMPIRICS.md) | Why `archy dsm` ships as visualization-only and no DSM-derived scalar becomes a score axis or diagnostic. |
| [`SCORE_SHAPE_REDESIGN_EMPIRICS.md`](SCORE_SHAPE_REDESIGN_EMPIRICS.md) | The 28-project study of acyclicity/depth reformulations and aggregator alternatives that concluded against any axis change. |
| [`ACYCLICITY_DILUTION_EMPIRICS.md`](ACYCLICITY_DILUTION_EMPIRICS.md) | The #192 decision: should `overall` be changed so a single cycle registers at scale? Corpus study of count-sensitive acyclicity terms; rejected (they penalize large near-acyclic codebases and duplicate the FP-free `cycles.added` signal). The dilution is documented as intended. Harness in `bench/acyclicity_dilution.py`. |
| [`TYPE_HINT_COVERAGE_EMPIRICS.md`](TYPE_HINT_COVERAGE_EMPIRICS.md) | The study that rejected type-hint coverage in both axis and diagnostic form. |
| [`AUTONOMY_CONTINUUM_SYNTHESIS.md`](AUTONOMY_CONTINUUM_SYNTHESIS.md) | Synthesis of Tracy Bannon's AI Autonomy Continuum talk: where archy sits on the continuum, the productivity-theater / score-gaming risk, and autonomy-tiered gating (deterministic checks may block, inferential checks stay advisory). Positioning and vocabulary, not new metrics. |
| [`AGENT_CAUSAL_REASONING_SYNTHESIS.md`](AGENT_CAUSAL_REASONING_SYNTHESIS.md) | Synthesis of Phroneses' "Agents Cannot Maintain Systems" (additive vs transformative gap), tested against the 2025-2026 causal-reasoning, fitness-function, and AI-PR-review literature. Frames archy as an externalized causal model; maps the article's five causal dimensions to archy's surface (gap analysis); proposes `archy_simulate` (counterfactual pre-edit check) for agent causal reasoning and a per-PR structural review brief for human judgment. Positioning and design input, not new metrics. |
| [`PREWALK_READ_REDUCTION_SYNTHESIS.md`](PREWALK_READ_REDUCTION_SYNTHESIS.md) | Synthesis of Stencil's "Prewalk" (the agent bill is `O(reads)`, not `O(edits)`) against archy's big question (#289): can an archy structural pre-edit brief reduce the exploratory reads an agent does before editing? Concludes prewalk's warm-trajectory handoff is not something a tool-mediated artifact can replicate (archy is weak for the handoff analogue), leaving only the substitution claim, which archy already half-ships (`invariant_brief`, `impact`, `graph(focus)`) but had never been measured. **Outcome: a documented non-result.** The #259 harness's arm-C extension ran to N=22 (`claude-sonnet-5`, flask); the brief did not reliably reduce reads-before-first-edit (pre_edit_reads median Δ −2.0, 14/8 pairs, sign p=0.286, after an N=10 hint at p=0.109 that did not survive more data). **NO-GO on any `archy brief` surface, now on evidence**, not an unproven prior (see `bench/agent_footprint_results.md`). |
| [`PATTERN_DETECTION_EMPIRICS.md`](PATTERN_DETECTION_EMPIRICS.md) | The #288 decision: can archy *infer* Cosmic Python's architectural patterns (Hexagonal, Repository, Service Layer, Message Bus, UoW/Aggregate/CQRS/DI) from the dependency graph? **NO-GO on evidence.** Four inferred detectors over three corpora (cosmicpython branches / framework-coupled controls / 29 general projects): purity-based is tautological (0 flags across 40 repos), the two position-based ones separate the corpora perfectly at repo level while identifying **zero true domain modules on 2 of the 3 controls** (they flag CLI entrypoints, translation adapters, exception modules) and cannot tell an inapplicable project from a violating one (they report hexagonal violations in django and flask themselves), and naming-based has the best domain precision but is a convention check, 52% vacuous, and blind to transitive coupling. A 14-line `.importlinter` contract with `include_external_packages = True` catches the case they all miss, with chains and line numbers, though on one repo and with the domain names handed to it. **Contracts win on transitivity**; the general reason inference fails is that "domain" is a statement of intent and the import graph does not carry intent. Harness `bench/pattern_detection.py`; the results file logs six corrections made after adversarial review overturned three first-run claims. |
| [`CONSTRAINT_AWARE_ORCHESTRATION_SYNTHESIS.md`](CONSTRAINT_AWARE_ORCHESTRATION_SYNTHESIS.md) | Answer to #298: should archy ship agent-framework integrations (LangGraph, Pydantic AI, CrewAI, OpenAI Agents SDK) to serve the DevDigest/Constraint-Decay call for "constraint-aware orchestration"? Finding: the gap the article names is **archy-side, not integration-side.** All four frameworks are already MCP clients and the remaining guard glue is 10-30 lines each, while the advisory-vs-hard-failure dial the article asks for is only half-built (`sdp.mode: warn\|error` proves the mechanism but is scoped to one built-in heuristic that is off by default; project-authored `forbid` rules have no severity at all). **Native adapters wontfix; docs recipe deferred behind a usage signal (zero inbound demand today); the gate bench not scheduled on cost** (its obvious endpoint is tautological, but three bounded-retry endpoints and a held-out-constraint design are not, all recorded). Two independently-justified archy-side items fall out: per-rule severity (#309) and a canned remediation string (#310). |
| [`INLOOP_PREVALENCE_EMPIRICS.md`](INLOOP_PREVALENCE_EMPIRICS.md) | Empirical answer to the synthesis's deepest open question. Replays 1,072 human-authored commits across 11 mature repos to measure how often a real change introduces a structural regression archy catches. Finding: new import cycles are rare per commit (0.5%) but concentrate in large changes (median 7x the files) and are severe when they fire; the composite score drops on 29% of commits but 98% of drops are sub-0.005 noise (validating the advisory-vs-blocking split). Reframes archy as a rare-firing, low-FP gate; specifies the agent A/B protocol for the remaining causal question. Harness in `bench/inloop_prevalence.py`. |

For *why we built what we built* (retrospective design rationale and competitive positioning), see [`../LEARNINGS.md`](../LEARNINGS.md). For the forward roadmap, see [`../ROADMAP.md`](../ROADMAP.md) and [`../FUTURE.md`](../FUTURE.md).

research: are the token-reduction claims real, and should archy build one? NO-GO

Survey of the token-reduction claims made by coding-agent tools, harnesses,
and skills, and the call for archy. Findings note
docs/research/TOKEN_REDUCTION_CLAIMS.md.

Sorting the category by MECHANISM rather than by product splits it cleanly:

PREFIX BLOAT (tool definitions) is the real half. Independently measured at
67,300 tokens across seven MCP servers, 33.7% of a 200k window, before the user
types anything. archy already solved its share in #227/#265 (19 tools to 11).
Measured archy's surface directly with tiktoken: 3,918 model-visible tokens,
1.96% of a 200k window, ~356 per tool, against GitHub MCP's ~18k for 27 tools.
Nothing left to build; Claude Code now defers MCP tools by default anyway.

COMPREHENSION CONTEXT (repo maps, briefs, symbol retrieval) is the half archy
tested and failed twice, and the survey makes that null look better rather than
worse. aider ships the canonical repo map and publishes NO token measurement
(its benchmark is 133 single-file Exercism exercises scored on pass rate);
serena asserts efficiency in prose. The one independent replication that did
measure compression (arXiv 2606.01326, SWE-bench Verified) reports 42% fewer
input tokens for a 12 PERCENTAGE POINT drop in resolution rate.

The famous percentages do not survive their baselines: Cloudflare's 99.9% is
against 2,500 endpoints at an estimated 1.17M tokens (a config that cannot be
run), Anthropic's 98.7% is arithmetic on one constructed example, jCodeMunch's
95% is against reading an entire repository. And prompt caching (cache hits at
0.1x) already took most of the cost win those numbers describe, overstating
real savings by up to 10x for anything cached.

Also resolves an apparent contradiction: codegraph, archy's closest analogue,
publishes a genuinely good benchmark (7 repos, 7 languages, median of 4 runs
per arm, 69% fewer tokens). It does not contradict archy's nulls because the
TASK CLASS differs: their agent answers one architecture question, where the
graph IS the answer; archy measured editing tasks, where the graph is a hint
and measured headroom was zero. That gives gate 4 its first real answer and is
recorded as the reopen path (a structural-Q&A arm with a correctness gate),
gated on a usage signal that does not exist today.

Verdict: NO-GO, no tickets filed. One draft error worth noting: an earlier pass
measured archy's full MCP payload at 18,345 tokens and called archy a major
bloat contributor. The Anthropic Messages API tool spec has no output-schema
field, so outputSchema (79% of that payload) is client-side and not model
context. Corrected number is 5x smaller and the claim is retracted in §7.

cat > /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-hosanglee-archy/9af56c8e-f399-435e-8ff9-ce8d99c2438e/scratchpad/pr_token.md <<'EOF'
## The question

Tools, harnesses, and skills all claim to reduce coding-agent token usage. What are those claims based on, and does it make sense for archy to build one?

**NO-GO. No tickets filed.** Findings note `docs/research/TOKEN_REDUCTION_CLAIMS.md`.

## The finding: sort by mechanism, and the category splits in two

### Half one: prefix bloat. Real, measured, and archy already did its share.

The one independently measured, non-vendor problem in the space: a community measurement on claude-code issue #11364 found **seven MCP servers consuming 67,300 tokens of tool definitions, 33.7% of a 200k window**, before the user types anything.

archy attacked exactly this in #227/#265 (19 tools to 11). I measured archy's surface directly with `tiktoken`:

| component | tokens |
|---|---|
| descriptions | 2,256 |
| `inputSchema` | 1,662 |
| **model-visible total** | **3,918 (1.96% of 200k, ~356/tool)** |

For comparison, GitHub MCP is ~18,000 tokens for 27 tools. Claude Code now defers MCP tools by default anyway. **Nothing left to build.**

### Half two: comprehension context. Unmeasured by its own vendors.

This is where repo maps, briefs, and symbol retrieval live, and where archy's two nulls came from. The survey makes those nulls look *better*, not worse:

- **aider** ships the canonical repo map (tree-sitter + graph ranking + `--map-tokens`) and publishes **no token measurement**. Its benchmark is **133 single-file Exercism exercises scored on pass rate**, the setting where a whole-repo map is least relevant.
- **serena** asserts efficiency in prose with no numbers.
- The one **independent replication** that measured compression (arXiv 2606.01326, SWE-bench Verified, GPT-5-mini) reports **42% fewer input tokens for a 12 percentage-point drop in resolution rate.**

As far as this survey found, **archy is the only party in this category that measured the mechanism and reported the result.**

## The headline percentages do not survive their baselines

| claim | baseline it is measured against |
|---|---|
| Cloudflare Code Mode **99.9%** | 2,500+ endpoints at an estimated **1.17M tokens**, a config that cannot be run |
| Anthropic code execution **98.7%** | **one constructed example** in a blog post |
| jCodeMunch **~95%** | **reading the entire repository** |
| Hrubec & Cito **42%** | SWE-bench Verified, full benchmark, and it costs 12pp of resolution rate |

Plus the confound nobody mentions: **prompt caching**. Cache hits bill at **0.1x**. Every headline above is uncached list-price arithmetic, which **overstates the real cost saving by up to 10x** for anything that would have been cached. archy's own harness independently hit this when `pre_edit_input_tokens` proved near-useless under caching.

## Why codegraph's strong benchmark does not contradict our nulls

`codegraph` is archy's closest analogue and publishes the best benchmark in the survey (7 repos, 7 languages, Claude Code headless, median of 4 runs per arm, honest about its own weak spots): 89% fewer tool calls, 69% fewer tokens.

The difference is **task class**:

| | codegraph | archy #282 / #289 |
|---|---|---|
| task | answer one **architecture question** | make a **code edit** |
| does the graph contain the answer? | **yes** | **no**, the agent must read code to write code |
| measured headroom | enormous | **zero** (`pre_edit_distinct_files` delta = 0) |

A dependency graph is an *answer* to a structural question and a *hint* for an editing task. Both benchmarks got the result their task class implies.

## The call

NO-GO on three independent grounds, any one sufficient: the available surface is spent (of ten categories only three are a static analyzer's to build; two are shipped, the third is measured null twice); the headline numbers do not survive their baselines; and the usage signal is zero.

**Reopen path recorded** (not scheduled): §8 gives gate 4 its first real answer, so the note specifies an "arm D" structural-Q&A bench with a pre-registered correctness gate, conditioned on a usage signal and on accepting that a positive result substantiates **existing tools**, not a new feature.

## A correction inside the note

An earlier pass measured archy's *full* MCP payload at 18,345 tokens and concluded archy was a major bloat contributor. The Anthropic Messages API tool spec carries `name`, `description`, `input_schema` and **no output-schema field**, so `outputSchema` (79% of that payload) is client-side and never reaches the model. Corrected figure is 5x smaller; §7 retracts the claim and states the residual uncertainty rather than hiding it.

Docs only, no code, no release.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF

That last one inverts the ticket: #261 was filed before the bench reported and proposed the pitch "archy = cheaper agent runs". We tested that twice and couldn't show it, so §14c.7 marks the framing superseded and records the rule instead.

**The token-reduction research** is PR [#314](https://github.com/hslee16/Archy/pull/314). **NO-GO, no tickets filed.**

The finding that organizes everything is to sort the category by mechanism rather than by product, at which point it splits in two:

**Prefix bloat is the real half**, independently measured at 67,300 tokens across seven MCP servers (33.7% of a 200k window). archy already solved its share in #227/#265, and I measured what's left with tiktoken: **3,918 model-visible tokens, 1.96% of a 200k window, ~356 per tool**, against GitHub MCP's ~18k for 27 tools. Nothing to build.

**Comprehension context is the half we already failed at**, and the survey makes our nulls look better rather than worse. aider ships the canonical repo map and publishes **no token measurement at all** (its benchmark is 133 single-file Exercism exercises scored on pass rate). serena asserts efficiency in prose. The one independent replication that actually measured compression reports **42% fewer input tokens for a 12-point drop in resolution rate**. As far as this survey found, archy is the only party in the category that measured the mechanism and published the result.

The famous percentages don't survive their baselines: Cloudflare's 99.9% is against a 1.17M-token configuration that cannot be run, Anthropic's 98.7% is arithmetic on one constructed example, jCodeMunch's 95% is against reading an entire repo. And prompt caching bills hits at 0.1x, so every one of those uncached-list-price numbers overstates real savings by up to 10x.

The most useful new insight: **codegraph's genuinely strong benchmark doesn't contradict our nulls, because the task class differs.** Their agent answers architecture questions, where the graph *is* the answer. Ours made code edits, where the graph is a hint and measured headroom was zero. That gives gate 4 ("why would it beat the null?") its first real answer, so I recorded a structural-Q&A bench as the reopen path, gated on a usage signal.

One correction worth flagging: mid-research I measured archy's *full* MCP payload at 18,345 tokens and had drafted a conclusion that archy is a major bloat contributor. Checking the Anthropic Messages API tool spec showed it carries no output-schema field, so `outputSchema` (79% of that payload) never reaches the model. The corrected number is 5x smaller and §7 retracts the claim rather than quietly fixing it.

ADVERSARIAL review of two docs changes in the archy repo at /Users/hosanglee/archy, branch alee/token-reduction-research (which contains both commits). Your job is to REFUTE the claims, not confirm them. Default to reporting a problem when uncertain. Do NOT edit any files.

Files: docs/research/TOKEN_REDUCTION_CLAIMS.md (the main target), docs/research/RESEARCH_METRICS.md §14c.7 (new subsection), docs/research/README.md (two index rows).

Attack these specifically. Use WebSearch/WebFetch to verify external claims against primary sources, and run code to verify the self-measurement.

1. **The self-measurement (§7 of TOKEN_REDUCTION_CLAIMS.md).** It claims archy's MCP surface is 3,918 "model-visible" tokens (descriptions + inputSchema), 1.96% of a 200k window, ~356/tool, with outputSchema (14,427 tok) excluded as client-side only. Reproduce it: `uv run --with tiktoken python` against `archy.mcp.create_server().list_tools()`. Then attack the REASONING: is it actually true that MCP outputSchema never reaches the model? Check the Anthropic Messages API tool spec and, more importantly, check what real MCP clients do. Does Claude Code fold outputSchema into the description? Does FastMCP? If any common client forwards it, the retraction in §7 is itself wrong and the original 18,345 figure was closer to right. Also: is cl100k_base the right tokenizer for a Claude model, and does using it materially bias the number?

2. **"aider publishes no token measurement."** This is load-bearing (it is used to argue archy is the only party that measured the mechanism). Verify hard: search aider's docs, blog, and GitHub for ANY published token/cost measurement of the repo map. If aider has ever published one, the claim is false and §2/§6/§8 all weaken.

3. **The minification paper (arXiv 2606.01326).** The note leans on "42% fewer input tokens, -12pp resolution rate" as the key independent evidence. Verify the numbers and, critically, the CHARACTERIZATION: is it fair to present this as evidence that compressing context costs capability in general? What exactly was minified (source code lexical elements?), on what agent framework, and does it actually generalize to repo maps and briefs the way the note implies? Is the note over-extending a specific result?

4. **The codegraph task-class argument (§8).** The note claims codegraph's 69%-fewer-tokens result does not contradict archy's nulls because codegraph measured "answering one architecture question" while archy measured editing. Verify codegraph's benchmark scope from its README. Then steelman the opposite: is this a real distinction or a convenient rationalization that lets archy off the hook? <result>## Verdict: the citation is REAL and the numbers check out. One framing problem, one date nit, and one significant scope caveat.

### (a) arXiv ID resolves, title and authors match exactly
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01326 resolves. Title: "Reducing Token Usage of State-in-Context Agents using Minification". Authors: **Nicolas Hrubec and Jürgen Cito**, both TU Wien. So "Hrubec & Cito" is correct.
- Code: https://github.com/ipa-lab/minified-state-in-context-agent
- Related prior artifact found: Hrubec's TU Wien diploma thesis "Reducing Token Usage of Software Engineering Agents" (repositum.tuwien.at), i.e. the paper is thesis-derived.

**Date nit (in the note's favor, actually):** submission history says **"[v1] Sun, 31 May 2026 16:24:22 UTC"**. So "(May 2026)" is *correct* for the submission date; the 2606 ID block is just where a 31-May-16:24-UTC submission lands after the announcement cutoff. Not a fabrication signal. No discrepancy to flag beyond explaining it.

### (b) The exact numbers: verified verbatim
Abstract: "Experiments show that minification reduces average input token usage by **42%** with a **12 percentage-point** drop in resolution rate."

Table 1 (SWE-bench Verified, GPT-5-mini):

| Run Type | Resolved | Resolved (%) | Avg. Input Tokens | Std |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| no-minification | 252 | 50.0 | 90,535 | 16,795 |
| minification | 188 | 38.0 | 52,776 | 13,697 |

Minor internal inconsistency worth knowing: 252 and 188 over SWE-bench Verified's 500 instances would be 50.4% and 37.6%, not the reported 50.0/38.0. Doesn't change the story.

### (c) What was minified: SOURCE CODE, lexically. All three of the note's guesses, plus more.
Section 3.2, built on `pyminifier` (Python only), transformations: **line/operator whitespace removal** (blank lines, spaces around operators), **comment/docstring removal**, **dedent**, **short identifiers** (variable/function/class renaming, with a reversible mapping table), **merge/remove imports**. Renaming is reversed in the SEARCH/REPLACE blocks post-generation, and patch application uses a matcher that "tolerates differences in whitespace, comments, and docstrings."

### (d) The scaffold: not SWE-agent, not mini-SWE-agent
"State-in-context" is Jiang et al. 2025, *"Putting it all into context: simplifying agents with LCLMs"*. > "An equivalent MCP server without Code Mode would consume 1.17 million tokens — more than the entire context window of the most advanced foundation models."

## 2. ANTHROPIC CODE EXECUTION WITH MCP — **PARTLY MISCHARACTERIZED**

https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/code-execution-with-mcp, "Published Nov 04, 2025".

Numbers verified verbatim, single occurrence each in the whole post ("98.7" appears 1×, "150,000" appears 1×):

> "This reduces the token usage from 150,000 tokens to 2,000 tokens—a time and cost saving of 98.7%."

**Where the note is right:** it is indeed ONE constructed worked example, Google Drive → Salesforce, with no benchmark, no N, no methodology. The 150,000 baseline is never derived — the closest support is a hand-wave two sections earlier: "In cases where agents are connected to thousands of tools, they'll need to process hundreds of thousands of tokens before reading a request."

**Where the note is wrong:** it attributes the 98.7% to the *transcript-passing-through-the-model-twice* mechanism. It is not. The 98.7% sentence sits at the end of the **tool-definition discovery** paragraph:

> "The agent discovers tools by exploring the filesystem... This lets the agent load only the definitions it needs for the current task. This reduces the token usage from 150,000 tokens to 2,000 tokens—a time and cost saving of 98.7%."

The double-pass problem is a *different* mechanism with a *different* number, in section "2. Intermediate tool results consume additional tokens":

> "In this example, the full call transcript flows through twice. For a 2-hour sales meeting, that could mean processing an additional 50,000 tokens."

**Headline or illustration?** Illustration. The post's headings are: two problem sections (tool definitions overload; intermediate results), one solution section, then "Benefits of code execution with MCP" with five sub-benefits (Progressive disclosure, Context efficient tool results, More powerful and context-efficient control flow, Privacy-preserving operations, State persistence and skills). The Summary contains no numbers at all. The 98.7% appears once, mid-post, and is not restated. So the note's framing of it as one illustration rather than a headline result is fair — but it pins it to the wrong mechanism.

---

## 3. ANTHROPIC TOOL SEARCH TOOL — **85% VERIFIED (with an arithmetic problem); 10%-threshold claim MISCHARACTERIZED**

### 85% figure — verified verbatim

https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/advanced-tool-use, "Published Nov 24, 2025". Appears exactly once:

> "Traditional approach: All tool definitions loaded upfront (~72K tokens for 50+ MCP tools) / Conversation history and system prompt compete for remaining space / Total context consumption: ~77K tokens before any work begins
> With the Tool Search Tool: Only the Tool Search Tool loaded upfront (~500 tokens) / Tools discovered on-demand as needed (3-5 relevant tools, ~3K tokens) / Total context consumption: ~8.7K tokens, preserving 95% of context window
> This represents an 85% reduction in token usage while maintaining access to your full tool library."

**Flag:** the 85% does not reconcile with its own stated baseline. 8.7K / 77K = 11.3%, i.e. an **88.7%** reduction; against the 72K definitions-only figure it is 87.9%. Neither yields 85%. The baseline is also a constructed five-server scenario (GitHub 35 tools ~26K, Slack 11 ~21K, Sentry 5 ~3K, Grafana 5 ~3K, Splunk 2 ~2K), not a measured workload.

The post's actually-measured claims are the accuracy ones, which the note omits: "Opus 4 improved from 49% to 74%, and Opus 4.5 improved from 79.5% to 88.1% with Tool Search Tool enabled."

https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/claude-code/mcp:

> "Tool search is enabled by default. MCP tools are deferred rather than loaded into context upfront, and Claude uses a search tool to discover relevant ones when a task needs them."
> "If you prefer threshold-based loading, set `ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=auto` to load schemas upfront when they fit within 10% of the context window and defer only the overflow."
> (table) "`auto` — Threshold mode: tools load upfront if they fit within 10% of the context window, deferred otherwise"

So: **ON by default — VERIFIED.** But the note's mechanism is wrong on two counts. (a) The default is unconditional deferral of *all* MCP tools, not threshold-triggered; there is no 10% test in the default path. (b) The 10% threshold is **opt-in** (`ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=auto`, or `auto:N` for a custom percentage) and is phrased as *load upfront when they fit WITHIN 10%* — the direction the fact-check asked about. The note's "auto-activates when descriptions exceed 10%" describes only the opt-in mode, and describes it as if it were the default. Also unmentioned: default is disabled on Google Cloud's Agent Platform and when `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` points to a non-first-party host.

## 4. jCodeMunch — **MISCHARACTERIZED (the N is fabricated; the percentages are misattributed)**

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jgravelle/jcodemunch-mcp/main/TOKEN_SAVINGS.md (7,708 bytes, read in full).

**"~95%+ on code-reading tasks" — verbatim present:**

This is an unsourced blanket assertion in the intro, tied to no table or measurement.

**The cited table row — the note misquotes the percentage.** The "Typical Savings by Task" table reads:

| Explore repo structure | ~200,000 tokens | ~2k tokens | ~99% |

## Part A — API tool-definition specs

### A1. Anthropic Messages API `tools` — NO output schema field

**Custom tool object fields** (from `docs.claude.com/en/docs/agents-and-tools/tool-use/implement-tool-use` and the advanced-tool-use engineering post):

- `name` (required)
- `description` (required, best-effort quality)
- `input_schema` (required — JSON Schema for the tool's **input** only)
- `type` (for built-in/Anthropic-defined tools like bash, text_editor, computer, memory; custom tools omit `type` or omit for "custom")
- `cache_control` — e.g. `{"cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}}`, prompt-caching breakpoint marker, unrelated to output
- `defer_loading` (beta, `advanced-tool-use-2025-11-20`) — for Tool Search Tool discovery
- `allowed_callers` (beta) — controls whether a tool can be invoked programmatically (Programmatic Tool Calling)
- `input_examples` (new field) — array of example **input** objects validated against `input_schema`

Quote from `implement-tool-use`:
> "Add an optional `input_examples` field to your tool definition with an array of example input objects. Each example must be valid according to the tool's `input_schema`"

Quote from the advanced-tool-use engineering doc (`www.anthropic.com/engineering/advanced-tool-use`):
```
{
  "name": "github.createPullRequest",
  "description": "Create a pull request",
  "input_schema": {...},
  "defer_loading": true
}
```

**Verdict: no output/result schema field exists on a custom tool object.** Every field found governs the tool's identity, input validation, caching, or discovery — none describe the tool's return shape.

**Structured outputs** (`docs.claude.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/structured-outputs`) is explicitly **response-level**, not per-tool:
> "Structured outputs provide two complementary features: **JSON outputs** (`output_config.format`): Get Claude's response in a specific JSON format. **Strict tool use** (`strict: true`): Guarantee schema validation on tool names and inputs."
> "**JSON outputs** control Claude's response format (what Claude says). **Strict tool use** validates tool parameters (how Claude calls your functions)."

`output_config` is a top-level request parameter (sibling to `messages`, `tools`), not a field inside a tool object:
```python
response = client.messages.create(
    ...
    output_config={"format": {"type": "json_schema", "schema": {...}}},
    ...
)
```
`strict: true` also only tightens `input_schema` compliance ("input" side), confirmed by OpenAI-parallel behavior and Anthropic's own framing above. **No per-tool output schema field exists in the Anthropic API.**

### A2. OpenAI — NO output schema field on function tools; hosted MCP also lacks it

From `platform.openai.com/docs/guides/function-calling`:
```json
{
    "type": "function",
    "function": {
        "name": "get_weather",
        "description": "Retrieves current temperature for the given location.",
        "strict": true,
        "parameters": {...}
    }
}
```
Fields: `type`, `name`/`function.name`, `description`, `parameters`, `strict`. `strict` "leverag[es] our structured outputs feature" but only constrains `parameters` (input): "`additionalProperties` must be set to `false` for each object in the `parameters`." No output/response schema field exists.

**Hosted MCP tool** (`type: "mcp"`, from `platform.openai.com/docs/guides/tools-connectors-mcp`):
```json
{
  "type": "mcp",
  "server_label": "dmcp",
  "server_url": "https://dmcp-server.deno.dev/mcp",
  "require_approval": "never",
  "allowed_tools": ["roll"]
}
```
Documented fields: `type`, `server_label`, `server_description`, `server_url`, `authorization`, `require_approval`, `allowed_tools`, `connector_id`. **No `outputSchema` field or reference appears anywhere in this doc page or in the tool-config surface** — the hosted MCP integration passes through server URL/auth/filtering config only; it does not surface or forward MCP `outputSchema`.

### A3. Google Gemini `FunctionDeclaration` — CONFIRMED: has `response`/`responseJsonSchema`

Quoted directly from `ai.google.dev/api/generate-content#FunctionDeclaration`:
> `response` `object (Schema)` — "Optional. Describes the output from this function in JSON Schema format. Reflects the Open API 3.03 Response Object. The Schema defines the type used for the response value of the function."
>
> `responseJsonSchema` `value (Value format)` — "Optional. Describes the output from this function in JSON Schema format. The value specified by the schema is..." (JSON-Schema-native counterpart, mutually exclusive with `response`, paralleling `parametersJsonSchema`/`parameters`)

Full field list on `FunctionDeclaration`: `name`, `description`, `behavior`, `parameters`, `parametersJsonSchema`, `response`, `responseJsonSchema`. **This is a genuine per-tool output schema field at the API level** — a real exception to Anthropic/OpenAI.

### A4. Gemini CLI (`google-gemini/gemini-cli`) — does NOT forward MCP `outputSchema` into it (refutation confirmed)

Two things exist in the repo:
1. `responseJsonSchema` appears in `packages/core/src/code_assist/converter.ts` and `packages/core/src/core/baseLlmClient.ts` — but these are strictly **response-level `GenerationConfig` fields**, siblings of `responseMimeType`/`responseSchema` (Gemini's whole-response "JSON output" feature), not tool-object fields:
```ts
// converter.ts
responseSchema: config.responseSchema,
responseJsonSchema: config.responseJsonSchema,
```
This mirrors GenerationConfig's JSON representation (`responseSchema`, `responseJsonSchema`, `responseMimeType`) documented on the same Gemini API page — unrelated to per-tool `response`.

2. The actual MCP→`FunctionDeclaration` conversion, in `packages/core/src/tools/mcp-client.ts` (`McpCallableTool.tool()`), explicitly maps only:
```ts
async tool(): Promise<Tool> {
  return {
    functionDeclarations: [
      {
        name: this.toolDef.name,
        description: this.toolDef.description,
        parametersJsonSchema: this.toolDef.inputSchema,
      },
    ],
  };
}
```
`this.toolDef.outputSchema` is **never read or mapped** to `response`/`responseJsonSchema` here. A `gh search code "outputSchema" --repo google-gemini/gemini-cli` turned up exactly one hit repo-wide, `packages/core/src/services/memoryService.test.ts: outputSchema: {}`, an unrelated test fixture — no production code path threads MCP `outputSchema` through.

**Verdict: confirmed refutation.** Even though Gemini's own API supports a per-tool output schema, Gemini CLI's MCP tool bridge discards `outputSchema` and only forwards `inputSchema`.

## Part B — IDE clients

### VS Code / GitHub Copilot Chat (`microsoft/vscode`) — validation/typing only, NOT forwarded to the model

`src/vs/platform/mcp/common/modelContextProtocol.ts` (and the mirrored copy in `extensions/copilot/src/extension/common/modelContextProtocol.ts`) contains the MCP spec's own type definitions, verbatim:
```ts
/**
 * An optional JSON Schema object defining the structure of the tool's output returned in
 * the structuredContent field of a {@link CallToolResult}.
 * ...
 */
outputSchema?: {
  $schema?: string;
  type: "object";
  properties?: { [key: string]: object };
  required?: string[];
};
```
and on the result side:
```ts
/**
 * If the tool defined an {@link Tool.outputSchema}, this SHOULD conform to that schema.
 */
structuredContent?: { [key: string]: unknown };
```

Critically, the file that actually builds the tool object VS Code hands to the language model — `src/vs/workbench/contrib/mcp/common/mcpLanguageModelToolContribution.ts` — only copies `inputSchema` into `IToolData`:
```ts
const toolData: IToolData = {
  id: tool.id,
  ...
  modelDescription: tool.definition.description ?? '',
  inputSchema: tool.definition.inputSchema,
  ...
};
```
`outputSchema` never appears in this construction. Downstream, `structuredContent` from a tool call result is just JSON-stringified and pushed into the model's context as text:
```ts
if (callResult.structuredContent) {
  details.output.push({ type: 'embed', isText: true, value: JSON.stringify(callResult.structuredContent, null, 2), ... });
  result.content.push({ kind: 'text', value: JSON.stringify(callResult.structuredContent), ... });
}
```
There is also a Codex-protocol type mirror (`src/vs/platform/agentHost/node/codex/protocol/generated/Tool.ts`) that likewise just types `outputSchema?: JsonValue` without further use found.

**Verdict: VS Code declares/types `outputSchema` (to stay MCP-spec-compliant and to type-check `structuredContent`), but does not map it into a per-tool "response schema" field it sends to the underlying model** — it only forwards `inputSchema`, and treats result `structuredContent` as opaque JSON text for the model to read, not schema-validated or advertised up front. Could not find any ajv/validation call against `outputSchema` in the files inspected — dedicated validation code (if any) was not located in this pass and should be treated as "could not determine" rather than ruled out.

<result>## Verdict: the conclusion is **mostly safe but the word "NEVER" is refuted**, and the **reasoning is invalid as written**

I found one real counter-example where MCP `outputSchema` reaches the model, and the note's argument has a structural flaw independent of that.

---

### 1. The stated premise is correct (Anthropic API)

Anthropic custom tool objects carry no output-schema field. Fields are `name`, `description`, `input_schema`, plus `type`, `cache_control`, `defer_loading`, `allowed_callers`, `input_examples`. "Structured outputs" does **not** change this: `output_config.format` is a *response-level* request parameter, and `strict: true` only tightens `input_schema`. Anthropic's docs draw the line explicitly:

> "JSON outputs control Claude's response format (what Claude says). Strict tool use validates tool parameters (how Claude calls your functions)."

Confirmed in Claude Code's own binary (v2.1.219), which is the exact serializer that builds the API payload:

```js
let d={name:u.name,description:u.description,input_schema:u.input_schema,
       ...u.strict&&{strict:!0},...u.eager_input_streaming&&{eager_input_streaming:!0}};
if(t.deferLoading)d.defer_loading=!0;
if(t.cacheControl)d.cache_control=t.cacheControl;
```

with an allowlist of `["name","description","input_schema","cache_control"]`. Its MCP→tool converter never reads `outputSchema` at all; the only MCP-related uses in the whole 250 MB binary are `cacheToolMetadata`/`validateToolOutput`, which compile it into an AJV validator for `structuredContent`. Notably, when Claude Code exposes its *own* tools as an MCP server it writes `outputSchema: void 0` outright.

### 2. The reasoning is invalid: it generalizes from one provider

The note argues "the Anthropic API has no output-schema field, **therefore** MCP `outputSchema` does not map into the model-visible tool spec." That inference fails because the premise is provider-specific. **Google's Gemini `FunctionDeclaration` does have a per-tool output schema field** — `response` / `responseJsonSchema`:

> "Optional. Describes the output from this function in JSON Schema format. The Schema defines the type used for the response value of the function." ([ai.google.dev/api/generate-content](https://ai.google.dev/api/generate-content))

So "no field in the Anthropic API" cannot carry the conclusion. (OpenAI matches Anthropic: `type`/`name`/`description`/`parameters`/`strict`, and their hosted `type: "mcp"` tool exposes no output-schema surface either.)

### 3. Actual refutation: google/adk-python forwards it, default-on

`src/google/adk/tools/mcp_tool/mcp_tool.py`:

```python
input_schema = self._mcp_tool.inputSchema
output_schema = self._mcp_tool.outputSchema
if is_feature_enabled(FeatureName.JSON_SCHEMA_FOR_FUNC_DECL):
    function_decl = FunctionDeclaration(
        name=self.name, description=self.description,
        parameters_json_schema=input_schema,
        response_json_schema=output_schema,   # <-- MCP outputSchema -> model-visible tool declaration
    )
```

I verified the gate is live, not dormant — `_feature_registry.py` line 170: `FeatureConfig(FeatureStage.EXPERIMENTAL, default_on=True)`. This is the third forwarding mode the note doesn't consider: not inlined text, but a genuine provider tool-definition field in the request.

### 4. Everything else checked: validation-only or dropped

| Client | `outputSchema` handling |
|---|---|
| Claude Code | Validation only (AJV on `structuredContent`); never in API payload |
| Anthropic Python SDK `mcp_tool()` | **Dropped** — maps `description` + `inputSchema` only; zero occurrences in the file |
| Vercel AI SDK `@ai-sdk/mcp` | Parses it in `ToolSchema`, then **never destructures it**; the `outputSchema` on the AI SDK tool comes from a user-supplied map, used only for `extractStructuredContent` validation |
| MCP Python SDK / TypeScript SDK | Validation only (`jsonschema.validate` / AJV) |
| LangChain MCP adapters | Dropped entirely (not even validated) |
| OpenAI Agents SDK | Dropped; description builder reads only `description`/`title` |
| mcp-use | Dropped entirely |
| FastMCP | Client: validation only. Proxy: protocol re-publication, not text injection |
| Gemini CLI | Dropped — `McpCallableTool.tool()` sets only `parametersJsonSchema`, despite the API supporting `responseJsonSchema` |
| VS Code / Copilot | Types it per spec; `mcpLanguageModelToolContribution.ts` copies only `inputSchema` into `IToolData` |
| Cursor | Could not determine (closed source) |

Independent empirical corroboration: a [July 2025 write-up](https://zenn.dev/7shi/articles/20250710-output-schema?locale=en) testing Claude Code and Gemini CLI concludes "current clients do not seem to look at that value," and found that even returned `structuredContent` isn't shown to the model — only `content` is.

### 5. Your token-accounting question

**`outputSchema` costs zero context in Claude Code.** Its per-MCP-tool budget computation counts exactly `{name, description, input_schema}`, and tool-search matching runs over name/description/`searchHint`. It is never in the payload, so it cannot be counted.

One caveat worth flagging: I found a widely-cited claim ([CrowdStrike falcon-mcp #325](https://github.com/CrowdStrike/falcon-mcp/issues/325), which shipped a fix omitting `outputSchema` from `tools/list`) asserting that VS Code Copilot's per-tool context budget *does* count `outputSchema`, causing silent tool drops. The issue provides no measurements, and reading the VS Code source contradicts it — only `inputSchema` reaches `IToolData`. Treat that as an unverified server-author inference, not evidence. A related real effect exists though: [claude-code #25081](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/25081) and [zed #55642](https://github.com/zed-industries/zed/issues/55642) show `outputSchema` causing tools to be *silently dropped* by clients — so it can have model-visible consequences by omission, just not by inclusion.

### 6. Spec position (weakly on the note's side, but quotable against it)

The 2025-06-18 spec's normative language is validation-only — "Servers **MUST** provide structured results that conform to this schema. Clients **SHOULD** validate structured results against this schema." But the same page's non-normative rationale says providing an output schema helps by "**Guiding clients and LLMs** to properly parse and utilize the returned data," which reads as anticipating model visibility. The current draft adds a sharper disclaimer: "`structuredContent` is server-produced result data and is unrelated to LLM 'structured outputs'."

---

### Recommended rewrite

The claim survives if scoped and re-derived. Something like:

> MCP `outputSchema` is consumed by the client rather than forwarded to the model in every Anthropic- and OpenAI-targeting client examined — those APIs' tool definitions carry only name, description, and input schema, so there is nowhere to put it. The exception is providers whose tool declaration has an output-schema field: Gemini's `FunctionDeclaration` exposes `responseJsonSchema`, and Google's ADK populates it directly from MCP `outputSchema` (default-on today), though Gemini CLI does not.

The specific edits: drop "NEVER"; stop deriving a protocol-wide conclusion from a single vendor's API shape; and note that "not forwarded" is an observed property of client implementations, not a consequence of the MCP spec.</result>

<result>The final check landed and it materially changes finding 15. Addendum:

## 16. §7 — the retraction's *conclusion* holds, but its *reasoning* is invalid, and there is a live counter-example

**The premise is confirmed.** Anthropic tool objects carry `name`, `description`, `input_schema` (plus `cache_control`, `defer_loading`, `strict`) and no output-schema field. Structured outputs does not change this: `output_config.format` is response-level, and `strict: true` only tightens `input_schema`. Verified in Claude Code's own serializer (v2.1.219), which builds the payload from an allowlist of `["name","description","input_schema","cache_control"]` and never reads `outputSchema` at all, using it only to compile an AJV validator for `structuredContent`. So **archy's 3,918 model-visible figure is correct on the dominant client, `outputSchema` costs it zero context, and the 18,345 retraction was right.**

**But the inference does not carry.** §7 argues "the Anthropic API has no output-schema field, **therefore** MCP `outputSchema` does not map into the model-visible tool spec." That is a provider-specific premise doing protocol-wide work. Gemini's `FunctionDeclaration` **does** have a per-tool output-schema field (`response` / `responseJsonSchema`: "Describes the output from this function in JSON Schema format"), and **google/adk-python populates it directly from MCP `outputSchema`**, default-on today:

```python
output_schema = self._mcp_tool.outputSchema
if is_feature_enabled(FeatureName.JSON_SCHEMA_FOR_FUNC_DECL):
    function_decl = FunctionDeclaration(..., response_json_schema=output_schema)
```

The gate is `FeatureStage.EXPERIMENTAL, default_on=True`, so it is live, not dormant. This is a third forwarding mode the note does not consider: not description-inlining, but a genuine provider tool-definition field.

Everything else surveyed drops it or validates only: Anthropic Python SDK `mcp_tool()`, Vercel AI SDK, MCP Python/TS SDKs, LangChain MCP adapters, OpenAI Agents SDK, mcp-use, FastMCP, Gemini CLI (which drops it despite the API supporting it), VS Code/Copilot. Cursor is closed-source and undetermined.

*Minimal correction to §7:* drop the derivation from the API shape; state it as an observed property of client implementations, not a consequence of the spec. Suggested replacement for the caveat paragraph: "`outputSchema` is consumed client-side rather than forwarded to the model in every Anthropic- and OpenAI-targeting client examined, including Claude Code, whose serializer allowlists `name`/`description`/`input_schema`. The exception is providers whose tool declaration has an output-schema field: Gemini's `FunctionDeclaration` exposes `responseJsonSchema` and Google's ADK populates it from MCP `outputSchema` by default."

Two further notes worth folding in. The spec's normative language is validation-only ("Clients SHOULD validate structured results against this schema"), which supports the note, but the same page's rationale says an output schema helps by "guiding clients and LLMs to properly parse and utilize the returned data," which is quotable against it. And a widely-cited claim (CrowdStrike falcon-mcp #325) that VS Code Copilot counts `outputSchema` toward its per-tool budget is **unverified and contradicted by the VS Code source** (only `inputSchema` reaches `IToolData`), so do not cite it. A real adjacent effect does exist though: claude-code #25081 and zed #55642 show `outputSchema` causing tools to be silently *dropped* by some clients, which is an archy-relevant risk given #228 ships it on all 11 tools, and which §9's "Trim `outputSchema` — **fails on premise**, wontfix" row does not account for.</result>

**The caveat that decides how to read this, and it matters.** The Anthropic
Messages API tool definition carries `name`, `description`, and `input_schema`.
There is **no output-schema field**. So MCP `outputSchema` (adopted in #228 for
`structuredContent`) does not map into the model-visible tool spec: a client
bridging MCP to the API consumes it for validation rather than forwarding it to
the model. An earlier draft of this section reported the 18,345 figure as
archy's context cost and called archy a major bloat contributor. **That was
wrong**, and the corrected number is 5x smaller.

input.new_string:
**The caveat that decides how to read this, and it matters.** MCP
`outputSchema` (adopted in #228 for `structuredContent`) is **consumed
client-side rather than forwarded to the model** in every Anthropic-targeting
and OpenAI-targeting client examined. Claude Code is the decisive case: its
serializer builds the tool payload from an allowlist of `name`, `description`,
`input_schema`, `cache_control`, and never reads `outputSchema` at all, using
it only to compile a validator for `structuredContent`. On the dominant client,
`outputSchema` costs archy **zero** context.

An earlier draft of this section reported the 18,345 figure as archy's context
cost and called archy a major bloat contributor. **That was wrong**, and the
corrected number is 5x smaller.

**But do not derive this from the API shape, which an earlier draft also did.**
"The Anthropic tool spec has no output-schema field, therefore MCP
`outputSchema` never reaches a model" is a provider-specific premise doing
protocol-wide work, and it is false in general. **Gemini's
`FunctionDeclaration` has a per-tool output-schema field**
(`responseJsonSchema`), and **google/adk-python populates it directly from MCP
`outputSchema`**, behind a feature gate that is default-on. So on a
Gemini-plus-ADK client, archy's 14,427 `outputSchema` tokens **do** enter the
tool declaration. The correct statement is an **observed property of client
implementations**, not a consequence of the spec. The MCP spec itself is
ambiguous in archy's favour but not decisively: its normative language is
validation-only ("Clients **SHOULD** validate structured results against this
schema"), while its rationale says an output schema helps guide "clients and
LLMs" to parse returned data.

Two related notes, since #228 ships `outputSchema` on all 11 tools:

- **A historical compatibility hazard, now closed.** Some clients silently
  dropped *every* tool from a server that sent `outputSchema`
  (anthropics/claude-code#25081, zed-industries/zed#55642). **Both are closed**,
  and archy's tools register correctly on current Claude Code, so this is not a
  live risk. It is worth knowing the failure mode is silent-total rather than
  degraded, because that is how it would present if it recurred.
- **A widely-circulated claim that VS Code Copilot counts `outputSchema`
  toward its per-tool budget is unverified** and contradicted by the VS Code
  source (only `inputSchema` reaches its tool data). Do not cite it.

  populates it from MCP `outputSchema` by default. The counter-example that
  makes §7 a client-implementation claim rather than a protocol one.
- [anthropics/claude-code#25081](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/25081),

Only the cancelled-cell sentence is wrong (2).

**No, and it does not warrant a ticket.** Concretely:

- **Claude Code: not affected.** Issue #25081 is **CLOSED (stale)**, was Windows-labelled, and its repro is the Kotlin SDK emitting the **MCP 2025-11-25** trio (`outputSchema` + tool-level `title` + `toolAnnotations`). archy emits 2025-06-18 `outputSchema`, and I verified directly this session that Claude Code registers and surfaces archy's tools normally. Zero cost too: Claude Code's per-MCP-tool budget counts only `{name, description, input_schema}`.
- **Zed: closed, upstream, low reach.** Issue #55642 is **CLOSED**, labelled `meta:upstream` / `severity:S3` / `reach:some users`, and the failure is specific to Zed forwarding MCP tools to an *external* agent over ACP (Copilot), not to Zed's own agent. Plausibly would have hit archy while open; no longer live.
- **Everything else surveyed drops or validates `outputSchema` without incident** (Anthropic SDK, Vercel AI SDK, MCP Python/TS SDKs, LangChain adapters, OpenAI Agents SDK, mcp-use, FastMCP, Gemini CLI, VS Code/Copilot). Cursor is closed-source and undetermined.
- **Do not cite CrowdStrike falcon-mcp #325** if this gets written up. Its claim that VS Code Copilot counts `outputSchema` toward a per-tool budget is unmeasured and contradicted by the VS Code source, where only `inputSchema` reaches `IToolData`.

The only doc consequence is that §9's D1 row "Trim `outputSchema` — **fails on premise**, wontfix" is correct on token grounds but rests on the flawed derivation in finding 9; fixing §7 fixes the row's justification without changing its verdict.</result>

The catalogue that informs the roadmap. |
8	| [`AXIS_REVIEW.md`](AXIS_REVIEW.md) | The OECD composite-indicator framework applied to every score-axis-promotion decision (why 5 axes, why `calls_per_edge` is not a 6th). |
